AL.summary: Refusing the evidentiary test after a DUI arrest isn't a crime in Alabama, but the state suspends your license, and no test is given unless police get a court order.
AL.inPractice: If you're later convicted of DUI, the refusal also means a required ignition interlock period (Ala. Code 32-5A-191). Officers can seek a warrant or court order for a blood test.
AL.detail: First refusal: 90-day suspension (1 year with one prior alcohol contact in 10 years)

AK.summary: Refusing a chemical test after a DUI arrest is its own crime in Alaska (a class A misdemeanor), separate from the DUI charge, and your license is revoked.
AK.inPractice: A first refusal conviction means at least 72 hours in jail, a $1,500 minimum fine, and 6 months of interlock. The refusal is admissible. Under Birchfield, this can apply to a breath-test refusal, not a blood test without a warrant.
AK.detail: First refusal: at least 90-day revocation, plus 72 hours in jail and a $1,500 fine if convicted

AZ.summary: In Arizona, refusing the test after a DUI arrest isn't a separate crime, but your license is suspended, and you must complete alcohol or drug screening to get it back.
AZ.inPractice: A second refusal within 84 months means a 2-year suspension. Failing to expressly agree to the test counts as a refusal. Officers can still seek a search warrant for a blood draw.

AR.summary: In Arkansas, refusing the chemical test is a separate 'violation' (a non-criminal, strict-liability offense) that brings a license suspension.
AR.inPractice: Some first-time refusers can get an ignition interlock restricted license right away. Based on FindLaw's copy of the statute (current as of March 2024); any fine amount wasn't confirmed.

CA.summary: Refusing isn't its own crime in California, but the DMV suspends or revokes your license, and if you're convicted of DUI, a breath or urine refusal adds penalties.
CA.inPractice: On a first DUI, a refusal means a 9-month DUI program instead of 3 months; other cases add 48 hours to 10 days of jail. Officers can require drivers under 21 to take a roadside PAS breath test.

sources.label: California DMV Driver's Handbook: Alcohol and Drugs

CO.summary: Colorado treats refusal as a license matter: refusing the test after a DUI arrest leads to revocation by the DMV, not a separate criminal charge.
CO.inPractice: Repeat refusals mean 2- and 3-year revocations. Officers can still seek a search warrant for blood. Based on FindLaw's copy of the statute (current as of January 2025).

CT.summary: Refusing the test after a DUI arrest isn't a separate crime in Connecticut, but it brings a license suspension and then a required ignition interlock, and the refusal can be used in court.
CT.inPractice: Refusing the non-testimonial part of a drug recognition evaluation also counts as a refusal. Repeat refusals mean 2 or 3 years of interlock. Officers can still seek a warrant for blood.
CT.detail: First refusal: 45-day suspension, then 1 year with an ignition interlock

DE.summary: Delaware handles refusal administratively: if you refuse the chemical test after a DUI arrest, your license is revoked. It isn't a separate crime.
DE.inPractice: Revocation is 18 or 24 months with prior DUI violations in 5 years. The law lets officers pursue testing without invoking implied consent, such as through a warrant, and requires testing after fatal crashes.

DC.summary: In D.C., refusing the chemical test after a DUI arrest isn't a separate crime, but it leads to license revocation (or a required ignition interlock program for D.C. license holders).
DC.inPractice: The refusal is admissible in court, and if you have a prior DUI-type conviction, refusing creates a presumption that you were impaired. Officers can still seek a warrant for blood.

FL.summary: Since Oct. 1, 2025 ('Trenton's Law'), refusing a breath or urine test after a lawful DUI arrest is a crime in Florida even the first time: a second-degree misdemeanor.
FL.inPractice: A second or later refusal is a first-degree misdemeanor. Officers must first warn you that refusal is a crime and suspends your license. The crime covers breath and urine tests; for blood, officers can seek a warrant.
FL.detail: First refusal: 1-year suspension (18 months for a later refusal)

GA.summary: Refusing state-administered testing after a DUI arrest isn't a crime in Georgia, but it brings a license suspension; some drivers can get an ignition interlock limited permit.
GA.inPractice: After Elliott v. State (2019), a breath-test refusal can't be used as evidence; the warning now says only blood or urine refusals may be used at trial. Based on FindLaw (current as of March 2024).

HI.summary: Hawaii no longer treats refusal as a crime, but refusing a breath, blood, or urine test after an OVUII arrest brings a longer license revocation than failing the test.
HI.inPractice: Hawaii repealed its petty-misdemeanor refusal law in 2016 after State v. Won (2015) held the threat of criminal penalties coerced consent. Refusal sanctions apply only if the officer gave the required warnings.

ID.summary: In Idaho, refusing evidentiary testing isn't a crime, but it brings a $250 civil penalty, a license suspension with no driving allowed, and a required ignition interlock afterward.
ID.inPractice: You have 7 days to request a court hearing to show cause for refusing. A second refusal within 10 years means a 2-year suspension. Officers can still seek a warrant for blood.
ID.detail: First refusal: 1-year absolute suspension and $250 civil penalty

IL.summary: Illinois doesn't make refusal a crime, but refusing the test after a DUI arrest triggers a 'statutory summary suspension' that is longer than the one for failing the test.
IL.inPractice: A first offender who fails the test gets 6 months; one who refuses gets 12 months, and non-first offenders who refuse get 3 years. Officers can still seek a warrant for blood.

IN.summary: Refusing a chemical test after an OWI stop isn't a separate crime in Indiana, but the BMV suspends your driving privileges.
IN.inPractice: The suspension is 2 years if you have a prior OWI conviction. Officers can still seek a search warrant for a blood draw. Based on FindLaw's copy of the statute (current as of January 2026).

IA.summary: Iowa treats refusal administratively: if you refuse chemical testing after an OWI arrest, your license is revoked, but refusal isn't its own crime.
IA.inPractice: A temporary restricted license is available only after you install an ignition interlock. A refusal with a prior revocation means 2 years. Officers can still seek a warrant for blood.

KS.summary: Kansas once made refusal a crime, but courts struck that law down and it was repealed in 2019. Today a refusal brings a license suspension and interlock, and it can be used at trial.
KS.inPractice: The Kansas Supreme Court held the criminal refusal law unconstitutional in State v. Ryce (2016, reaffirmed 2017). Officers can still get a warrant for blood. The roadside screening law sets no refusal penalty.
KS.detail: First refusal: 1-year suspension, then 2 years of ignition interlock

KY.summary: Refusal isn't a separate crime in Kentucky, but the court suspends your license at arraignment, the refusal can be used as evidence, and it can double jail time on a repeat DUI.
KY.inPractice: For a second or third DUI within 10 years, refusing doubles the mandatory minimum jail term; it isn't an aggravator on a first offense. Officers must seek a blood warrant after a fatal crash.
KY.detail: First refusal: license suspended by the court at arraignment

LA.summary: A first refusal in Louisiana leads to a license suspension, but refusing after two previous refusals is a crime that carries jail time.
LA.inPractice: That third refusal carries 10 days to 6 months in jail and a $300-$1,000 fine (R.S. 14:98.7). After crashes with death or serious injury, officers must direct a test. Based on FindLaw (current as of 2023).

ME.summary: Refusal isn't its own crime in Maine, but it brings a long license suspension, and if you're convicted of OUI, refusing adds mandatory jail time and a higher fine.
ME.inPractice: A first OUI with a refusal carries at least 96 hours in jail and a $600 minimum fine. Repeat offenders also get longer jail terms. Officers can still seek a warrant for blood.

MD.summary: In Maryland, refusal brings an administrative license suspension, and if you're convicted of DUI and found to have knowingly refused, you face up to 2 more months in jail and a $500 fine.
MD.inPractice: The extra refusal penalty applies only if the prosecutor gives notice before a plea or trial (Transp. § 21-902). A second refusal means a 2-year suspension.

MA.summary: Massachusetts suspends your license if you refuse the breath test after an OUI arrest, but refusal isn't a crime, and the refusal can't be used against you at trial.
MA.inPractice: State law makes refusal evidence inadmissible in criminal and civil cases, except license proceedings. Suspensions are much longer if you're under 21 or have prior OUI convictions.

MI.summary: Michigan doesn't make refusing the evidentiary test after arrest a crime, but it leads to a license suspension.
MI.inPractice: The roadside preliminary breath test (PBT) is different: refusing it is a civil infraction, like a ticket. A second evidentiary refusal within 7 years means 2 years. Officers can still seek a warrant for blood.

MN.summary: In Minnesota, refusing a breath test after a DWI arrest, or a blood or urine test ordered by a search warrant, is a crime, even on a first offense.
MN.inPractice: Test refusal is charged as third-degree DWI, a gross misdemeanor. After 2016 state supreme court rulings, a 2017 change limited blood or urine refusal crimes to cases with a warrant.

MS.summary: Refusing the chemical test after a DUI arrest isn't a crime in Mississippi, but the Department of Public Safety suspends your license.
MS.inPractice: With a prior DUI conviction or nonadjudication, the suspension is 1 year. Interlock-restricted driving is possible if a court orders it. Based on FindLaw (current as of January 2025).

MO.summary: In Missouri, your license is revoked right away if you refuse a chemical test after a DWI arrest. Refusal isn't a separate crime, but it's admissible in court.
MO.inPractice: If you have a prior alcohol-related enforcement contact, you need an ignition interlock for at least 6 months after reinstatement. Officers can still seek a warrant for blood.

MT.summary: Montana suspends your license, with no restricted license available, if you refuse the required test after a DUI arrest. Refusal isn't a separate crime.
MT.inPractice: After a refusal, the officer may apply for a search warrant to take a blood or oral fluid sample. Refusing both the roadside screening and the main test counts as one refusal. Based on FindLaw (2024).
MT.detail: First refusal: 6-month suspension (12 months for a second within 5 years)

NE.summary: Nebraska makes refusing a chemical test after a DUI arrest a separate crime, punished on the same scale as DUI, on top of an administrative license revocation.
NE.inPractice: Refusing the roadside preliminary breath test is also a misdemeanor (Class V) and leads to arrest. Under Birchfield (2016), criminal refusal charges hold for breath tests but not warrantless blood tests.

NV.summary: Refusing an evidentiary test after a DUI arrest isn't a crime in Nevada, but your license is revoked and you must install an ignition interlock on any vehicle you drive meanwhile.
NV.inPractice: After a refusal, the officer may apply for a warrant or court order allowing reasonable force to draw blood. A refusal within 7 years of a prior refusal revocation means 3 years.

NH.summary: New Hampshire suspends your license if you refuse the test after a DUI arrest; refusal itself isn't a crime.
NH.inPractice: With a prior DWI conviction or refusal, the suspension is 2 years. A change taking effect Jan. 1, 2027 raises these to 9 months for a first refusal and 3 years for repeats. Officers can still seek a warrant.
NH.detail: First refusal: 180-day suspension (9 months starting Jan. 1, 2027)

NJ.summary: In New Jersey, refusing a breath test is a separate traffic offense (not a crime) decided in municipal court, with fines, loss of your license, and an ignition interlock.
NJ.inPractice: Under a 2019 law, a first refusal brings a $300-$500 fine, an Intoxicated Driver Resource Center referral, and 9-15 months of interlock. Confirmed from the 2019 law text, not the current code.
NJ.detail: First refusal: license forfeited until an interlock is installed, then 9-15 months with it

NM.summary: New Mexico revokes your license for refusing the test, and if you're convicted of DWI, the refusal makes it 'aggravated DWI' with mandatory jail.
NM.inPractice: A first aggravated DWI carries at least 48 consecutive hours in jail. In State v. Vargas (2017), the state supreme court held refusing a warrantless blood test can't support aggravated DWI. Based on FindLaw (2024).

NY.summary: New York doesn't make refusal a crime, but refusing a chemical test after a DWI arrest leads to license revocation and a $500 civil penalty.
NY.inPractice: The refusal can be used at trial only if you were clearly warned of its effect and still refused. Revocation is 18 months with a prior refusal or DWI in 5 years. Officers can still seek a warrant.
NY.detail: First refusal: at least 1-year revocation and $500 civil penalty

NC.summary: In North Carolina, you can refuse any test, but your license is revoked and the refusal can be used as evidence at trial. Refusal isn't a separate crime.
NC.inPractice: The official rights notice warns that an officer can compel testing under other laws, such as with a search warrant. Revocations can be longer in some situations.

ND.summary: North Dakota makes refusing a chemical test after a DUI arrest a crime (a class B misdemeanor for a first offense). This is the law at the center of Birchfield v. North Dakota.
ND.inPractice: After Birchfield, criminal penalties hold for breath-test refusals, not warrantless blood tests. Refusing the roadside screening test can also cost your license unless you take the later chemical test.

OH.summary: For a first OVI arrest in Ohio, refusal brings a 1-year administrative suspension; with a prior OVI in 20 years, refusing becomes part of a tougher OVI charge.
OH.inPractice: Under R.C. 4511.19(A)(2), an impaired driver with a prior OVI who refuses faces high-tier penalties, such as 20 days of mandatory jail on a second offense. Officers can still seek a warrant.

OK.summary: Oklahoma doesn't make refusal a crime, but refusing a breath or blood test after a DUI arrest leads to revocation and the Impaired Driver Accountability Program (IDAP).
OK.inPractice: IDAP requires an ignition interlock. After a refusal, no test is given unless officers get a search warrant or believe you caused a death or serious injury.
OK.detail: First refusal: at least 180-day revocation and until IDAP is completed

OR.summary: In Oregon, refusing a breath or urine test isn't a crime, but it's a traffic violation with a $650 presumptive fine, plus a license suspension.
OR.inPractice: Evidence of a refusal is admissible in court. Suspensions are longer if you have a recent prior. Officers can still seek a warrant for a blood draw.

PA.summary: Refusal isn't a separate crime in Pennsylvania, but PennDOT suspends your license, and if you're convicted of DUI, a breath refusal puts you in the highest penalty tier.
PA.inPractice: A first DUI with a breath refusal, or refusing blood under a warrant, means at least 72 hours in jail and a $1,000-$5,000 fine. Refusing a warrantless blood test doesn't trigger this.
PA.detail: First refusal: 12-month suspension (18 months with priors)

RI.summary: A first refusal in Rhode Island is a civil offense, but a second refusal of a breath test within 10 years is a misdemeanor that can mean up to 6 months in jail.
RI.inPractice: A first refusal brings a $200-$500 fine, 10-60 hours of community service, a DWI course, and a $500 assessment. Blood-test refusals stay civil even when repeated.

SC.summary: South Carolina suspends your license if you refuse the test after a DUI arrest. Refusal isn't a crime, but it can be used against you in court.
SC.inPractice: You can end the suspension early by enrolling in the Ignition Interlock Device Program. Officers can still seek a warrant for a blood draw.

SD.summary: South Dakota revokes your license if you refuse chemical testing after a DUI arrest, and the refusal can be used at trial. It isn't a separate crime.
SD.inPractice: The state may let you drive for work during the revocation. You have 120 days from arrest to request a hearing. Officers can still seek a search warrant for blood.

TN.summary: In Tennessee, a court decides whether you violated the implied consent law. A violation isn't a criminal offense, but it means losing your license.
TN.inPractice: Revocations are longer with a prior DUI (2 years) or a crash causing serious injury or death (2-5 years). After injury crashes, officers test via warrant or exigency. Based on FindLaw (Jan. 2024).

TX.summary: Refusing a breath or blood test after a DWI arrest isn't a crime in Texas, but your license is suspended, and the refusal can be introduced at your trial.
TX.inPractice: Suspensions are longer if you have prior alcohol-related contacts. Officers can seek a search warrant for a blood draw after a refusal. Based on FindLaw (current as of January 2026).

UT.summary: Utah revokes your license if you refuse a chemical test after a DUI arrest. Refusal isn't a separate crime.
UT.inPractice: Under the version effective July 1, 2026, you may get your license back after 90 days if you're in a 24-7 sobriety program and use an interlock. With a prior in 10 years, it's 36 months.

VT.summary: For most first-time drivers, refusing an evidentiary test in Vermont brings a civil license suspension. But refusing is a crime if you have a prior DUI conviction or were in a crash causing serious injury or death.
VT.inPractice: During a refusal suspension, eligible drivers may drive with an ignition interlock license or certificate. Officers can still seek a warrant for a blood draw.

VA.summary: A first refusal of the breath test in Virginia is a civil offense, but refusing again within 10 years of a prior refusal or DUI conviction is a Class 1 misdemeanor.
VA.inPractice: Blood-test refusals are always civil. The court's suspension is added to the administrative suspension at arrest. A criminal repeat refusal means a 3-year loss of driving privileges.

WA.summary: Washington revokes your license if you refuse the test after a DUI arrest, and if you're convicted, a refusal puts you in the same higher penalty tier as a 0.15+ BAC.
WA.inPractice: For a first offense, that means at least 48 hours in jail instead of 24 (or alternatives like home monitoring) and higher fines. A second refusal within 7 years means a 2-year revocation.

WV.summary: In West Virginia, a court decides at a 'refusal review hearing' whether you refused the secondary chemical test; if so, the DMV revokes your license. Refusal isn't its own crime.
WV.inPractice: You can take back a refusal within 15 minutes. You have 30 days after your first court appearance to request the hearing. You may choose 45 days plus a year in the interlock program instead.
WV.detail: First refusal: 1-year revocation, or 45 days plus 1 year of interlock

WI.summary: Wisconsin revokes your operating privilege after an improper refusal of a chemical test. Refusal isn't a crime, but the refusal can be used against you in court.
WI.inPractice: You can get an occupational license after 30 days; a change effective Sept. 1, 2027 instead ties it to installing an interlock. Repeat refusals mean 2 or 3 years.

WY.summary: Wyoming is unusual: since 2011, refusing a chemical test doesn't automatically suspend a regular driver's license. Instead, officers can get a search warrant, even remotely, to test you.
WY.inPractice: Testing without consent is also allowed after crashes causing serious injury or death. Commercial drivers who refuse are disqualified from driving commercial vehicles.
WY.detail: First refusal: no automatic suspension for non-commercial drivers
